danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 1
paragraphs: Fra slutningen af 1811 tog en intensiveret oprustning og samling af Vesteuropas styrker til, og i 1812 bevægede disse styrker — millioner af mænd, medregnet dem, der transporterede og forsynede hæren — sig fra vest mod øst til den russiske grænse, hvorimod russiske styrker på lignende vis var blevet trukket sammen siden 1811. Den tolvte juni 1812 krydsede Vesteuropas styrker den russiske grænse, og krigen begyndte — det vil sige, en begivenhed indtraf, der var i modstrid med menneskelig fornuft og menneskelig natur. Millioner af mænd begik mod hinanden sådanne utallige forbrydelser, bedragerier, forræderier, tyverier, falsknerier, udstedelse af falske penge, indbrud, brandstiftelser og mord, som i hele århundreder ikke opregnes i alle verdens domstole, men som de, der begik dem, ikke dengang betragtede som forbrydelser.

Hvad frembragte denne ekstraordinære begivenhed? Hvad var dens årsager? Historikerne fortæller os med naiv sikkerhed, at dens årsager var de krænkelser, der var påført hertugen af Oldenburg, den manglende overholdelse af Kontinentalsystemet, Napoleons ærgerrighed, Alexanders fasthed, diplomaternes fejltagelser og så videre.

Følgelig ville det kun have været nødvendigt, at Metternich, Rumjantsev eller Talleyrand mellem en leveé og et aftenselskab havde gjort sig den rette umage og skrevet en mere behændig note, eller at Napoleon havde skrevet til Alexander: »Min ærede broder, jeg indvilliger i at give hertugdømmet tilbage til hertugen af Oldenburg« — og der ville ikke have været nogen krig.

Vi kan forstå, at sagen forekom samtiden sådan. Det var naturligt, at det for Napoleon syntes, at krigen var forårsaget af Englands intriger (som han faktisk sagde på øen Sankt Helena). Det var naturligt, at det for medlemmerne af det engelske parlament syntes, at krigens årsag var Napoleons ærgerrighed; for hertugen af Oldenburg, at krigens årsag var den vold, der var begået mod ham; for forretningsfolk, at krigens årsag var Kontinentalsystemet, der ødelagde Europa; for generalerne og de gamle soldater, at hovedårsagen til krigen var nødvendigheden af at give dem beskæftigelse; for legitimisterne af den tid, at det var behovet for at genoprette les bons principes; og for datidens diplomater, at det hele skyldtes, at alliancen mellem Rusland og Østrig i 1809 ikke var blevet tilstrækkeligt godt skjult for Napoleon, og at Memorandum nr. 178 var klodset formuleret. Det er naturligt, at disse og et utal af andre grunde, hvis antal afhænger af de synsvinklers uendelige mangfoldighed, fremstod for datidens mennesker; men for os, for eftertiden, der betragter det skete i hele dets omfang og opfatter dets klare og forfærdelige mening, forekommer disse årsager utilstrækkelige. For os er det uforståeligt, at millioner af kristne mennesker dræbte og pinte hinanden enten fordi Napoleon var ærgerrig eller Alexander var fast, eller fordi Englands politik var snedig, eller hertugen af Oldenburg blev krænket. Vi kan ikke fatte, hvad forbindelse sådanne omstændigheder har med selve den faktiske slagtning og vold: hvorfor tusinder af mennesker fra den anden side af Europa, fordi hertugen blev krænket, dræbte og ødelagde Smolensks og Moskvas folk og blev dræbt af dem.

For os, deres efterkommere, der ikke er historikere og ikke rives med af forskningens proces og derfor kan betragte begivenheden med ufordunklet sund fornuft, præsenterer et uberegneligt antal årsager sig. Jo dybere vi graver efter disse årsager, desto flere finder vi; og hver enkelt årsag eller hel kæde af årsager forekommer os lige gyldig i sig selv og lige falsk i sin ubetydelighed sammenlignet med begivenhedernes omfang og i sin afmagt — uden samvirke med alle de andre sammenfaldende årsager — til at fremkalde begivenheden. For os synes en fransk korporals ønske eller ulyst til at tjene en anden termin lige så meget som en årsag som Napoleons nægtelse af at trække sine tropper tilbage bag Wisła og gengive hertugdømmet Oldenburg; for havde han ikke ønsket at tjene, og havde en anden, en tredje og en tusindende korporal og menig også nægtet, ville der have været så mange færre mænd i Napoleons hær, at krigen ikke kunne have fundet sted.

Havde Napoleon ikke taget anstød af kravet om at trække sig bag Wisła og ikke beordret sine tropper fremad, ville der ikke have været nogen krig; men havde alle hans sergenter nægtet at tjene en anden termin, ville der heller ikke have været nogen krig. Der kunne heller ikke have været krig, hvis der ikke havde været nogen engelske intriger og ingen hertug af Oldenburg, og hvis Alexander ikke havde følt sig fornærmet, og hvis der ikke havde været et enevældigt styre i Rusland, eller en revolution i Frankrig og et derpå følgende diktatur og kejserrige, eller alle de ting, der frembragte den franske revolution, og så videre. Uden hver eneste af disse årsager ville intet have kunnet ske. Alle disse årsager — myriader af årsager — faldt altså sammen om at frembringe det. Og der var derfor ingen enkelt årsag til den begivenhed, men den måtte ske, fordi den måtte ske. Millioner af mennesker, der frasagde sig deres menneskelige følelser og fornuft, måtte gå fra vest mod øst for at slagte deres medmennesker, ligesom nogle århundreder tidligere horder af mænd var kommet fra øst mod vest og slagtede deres medmennesker.

Napoleons og Alexanders handlinger, på hvis ord begivenheden syntes at bero, var lige så lidet frivillige som enhver soldats, der blev trukket ind i felttogen ved lodtrækning eller værnepligt. Det kunne ikke være anderledes, for for at Napoleons og Alexanders vilje (som begivenheden syntes at afhænge af) kunne fuldbyrdes, var det nødvendigt, at millioner af omstændigheder faldt sammen, uden hvilke begivenheden ikke kunne have fundet sted. Det var nødvendigt, at millioner af mennesker, i hvis hænder den virkelige magt lå — soldaterne, der skød, eller transporterede forsyninger og kanoner — indvilligede i at udføre disse svage individers vilje og var blevet tilskyndet hertil af et uendeligt antal mangfoldige og komplekse årsager.

Vi er tvunget til at ty til fatalisme som forklaring på irrationelle begivenheder (det vil sige begivenheder, hvis fornuftsmæssighed vi ikke forstår). Jo mere vi forsøger at forklare sådanne begivenheder i historien fornuftigt, desto mere ufornuftige og uforståelige bliver de for os.

Hvert menneske lever for sig selv og bruger sin frihed til at nå sine personlige mål og føler med hele sin væren, at det nu kan gøre eller undlade at gøre denne eller hin handling; men så snart det har gjort det, bliver den handling, der er udført i et bestemt tidspunkt, uigenkaldelig og tilhører historien, hvori den ikke har en fri, men en forudbestemt betydning.

Der er to sider af ethvert menneskes liv: dets individuelle liv, som er desto friere, jo mere abstrakte dets interesser er, og dets elementære biliv, hvori det uundgåeligt adlyder love, der er fastlagt for det.

Mennesket lever bevidst for sig selv, men er et ubevidst redskab til opnåelse af menneskehedens historiske, universelle mål. En udført handling er uigenkaldelig, og dens resultat, der i tid falder sammen med millioner af andre menneskers handlinger, antager historisk betydning. Jo højere et menneske står på den sociale rangstige, jo flere mennesker det er forbundet med, og jo mere magt det har over andre, desto mere tydelig er forudbestemmelsen og uundgåeligheden af dets enhver handling.
»Kongens hjerte er i Herrens hånd.«
En konge er historiens slave.
Historien, det vil sige menneskehedens ubevidste, generelle biliv, bruger hvert øjeblik af kongernes liv som redskab til sine egne formål.

Skønt Napoleon på det tidspunkt, i 1812, var mere overbevist end nogensinde om, at det afhang af ham, om han ville udgyde (eller ikke udgyde) sine folks blod — som Alexander udtrykte det i det sidste brev, han skrev ham — havde han aldrig været så meget i greb af de uundgåelige love, der tvang ham, mens han troede, han handlede af egen fri vilje, til at udføre det for bilivets — det vil sige for historiens — nødvendige.
»At udgyde (eller ikke udgyde) sine folks blod.«

Vestens folkeslag bevægede sig østpå for at slagte deres medmennesker, og ifølge sammenfaldets lov passede tusinder af små årsager ind og samvirkede til at frembringe den bevægelse og krig: bebrejdelser for den manglende overholdelse af Kontinentalsystemet, hertugen af Oldenburgs krænkelser, troppebevægelserne ind i Preussen — foretaget (som det forekom Napoleon) kun for at sikre en bevæbnet fred — den franske kejsers kærlighed til og vane med krig, der faldt sammen med hans folks tilbøjeligheder, fristelsen fra forberedelsernes storhed og udgifterne til disse forberedelser og behovet for at opnå fordele, der kompenserede for de udgifter, de berusende æresbevisninger, han modtog i Dresden, de diplomatiske forhandlinger, som i samtidiges øjne førtes med et oprigtigt ønske om at opnå fred, men som kun sårede begge parters selvfølelse, og millioner af andre årsager, der tilpassede sig den begivenhed, der var ved at ske, eller faldt sammen med den.

Når et æble er modent og falder, hvorfor falder det da? På grund af sin tiltrækning til jorden, fordi stilken visner, fordi det tørres af solen, fordi det bliver tungere, fordi vinden ryster det, eller fordi drengen, der står nedenunder, ønsker at spise det?

Intet er årsagen. Alt dette er blot sammenfald af betingelser, under hvilke alle livsvigtige organiske og elementære begivenheder indtræffer. Og botanikeren, der finder, at æblet falder, fordi cellevævet nedbrydes og så videre, har lige så ret som barnet, der står under træet og siger, at æblet faldt, fordi han ønskede at spise det og bad om det. Lige ret eller uret har den, der siger, at Napoleon gik til Moskva, fordi han ville det, og gik til grunde, fordi Alexander ønskede hans undergang, og den, der siger, at en undermineret bakke, der vejer en million tons, faldt, fordi den sidste arbejder slog på den for sidste gang med sin hakke. I historiske begivenheder er de såkaldte store mænd etiketter, der giver navne til begivenheder, og ligesom etiketter har de kun den mindste forbindelse med selve begivenheden.
Enhver af deres handlinger, der for dem selv fremtræder som en handling af deres egen vilje, er i historisk forstand ufrivillig og knyttet til hele historiens gang og forudbestemt fra evighed.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: From the end of 1811, Western Europe armed and massed its forces more and more intensely, and in 1812 those forces — millions of men, counting the ones who carried supplies and fed the army — set out from the west and moved east toward the Russian frontier. Since 1811 the Russian forces had been drawn toward that same frontier. On the twelfth of June, 1812, the forces of Western Europe crossed it and war began. In other words, something happened that ran against human reason and human nature. Millions of men committed against one another countless crimes, frauds, betrayals, thefts, forgeries, issues of counterfeit money, burglaries, arsons, and murders — more than the records of all the law courts in the world could hold in whole centuries — and at the time the men who committed them did not regard them as crimes.

What produced this extraordinary event? What were its causes? The historians tell us, with naive assurance, that its causes were the wrongs done to the Duke of Oldenburg, the failure to observe the Continental System, Napoleon's ambition, Alexander's firmness, the mistakes of the diplomats, and so on.

It follows that Metternich, Rumyantsev, or Talleyrand, between a levee and an evening party, would only have needed to take proper pains and write a cleverer note, or Napoleon would only have needed to write to Alexander: "My respected Brother, I consent to restore the duchy to the Duke of Oldenburg" — and there would have been no war.

We can understand why the matter looked like that to people at the time. It naturally seemed to Napoleon that the war was caused by England's intrigues (as in fact he said on the island of St. Helena). It naturally seemed to members of the English Parliament that the cause was Napoleon's ambition; to the Duke of Oldenburg, that it was the violence done to him; to businessmen, that it was the Continental System, which was ruining Europe; to the generals and old soldiers, that the chief reason was the need to give them employment; to the legitimists of that day, that it was the need to re-establish les bons principes; and to the diplomats of that time, that it all came from the alliance between Russia and Austria in 1809 not having been hidden well enough from Napoleon, and from the clumsy wording of Memorandum No. 178. It is natural that these reasons, and a countless, endless number of others, their number depending on the endless variety of points of view, presented themselves to the men of that day. But to us, their posterity, who see what happened in all its magnitude and perceive its plain and terrible meaning, these causes seem insufficient. We find it incomprehensible that millions of Christian men killed and tortured one another because Napoleon was ambitious or Alexander was firm, or because England's policy was shrewd or the Duke of Oldenburg was wronged. We cannot grasp what connection such circumstances have with the actual fact of slaughter and violence: why, because the Duke was wronged, thousands of men from the other side of Europe killed and ruined the people of Smolensk and Moscow, and were killed by them.

For us, their descendants, the case is different. We are not historians, and the work of research has not carried us away, so we can look at the event with clear common sense, and what we see is an incalculable number of causes. The deeper we dig for causes, the more we find. Each single cause, or whole series of causes, strikes us as equally valid in itself, and equally false: it is insignificant beside the magnitude of the event, and by itself — without all the other causes that coincided with it — it is powerless to bring the event about. To us, a French corporal's wish or reluctance to serve a second term is as much a cause as Napoleon's refusal to withdraw his troops beyond the Vistula and restore the duchy of Oldenburg. For if that corporal had not wished to serve, and a second, a third, and a thousandth corporal and private had refused as well, Napoleon's army would have been that many men smaller and the war could not have happened.

There would have been no war if Napoleon had not taken offense at the demand to withdraw beyond the Vistula and had not ordered his troops forward; but if all his sergeants had objected to a second term, there could have been no war either. Nor could there have been one without England's intrigues and the Duke of Oldenburg, or if Alexander had not felt insulted, or if Russia had had no autocratic government, or France no Revolution and no dictatorship and Empire after it, or none of the things that produced the French Revolution, and so on. Take away any one of these causes and nothing could have happened. So all of them — myriads of causes — coincided to bring it about. There was no single cause of that event; it had to happen simply because it had to. Millions of men, giving up their human feelings and reason, had to go from west to east and slay their fellows, just as some centuries earlier hordes of men had come from the east to the west, slaying their fellows.

Napoleon and Alexander, on whose words the event seemed to hang, acted no more voluntarily than any soldier drawn into the campaign by lot or by conscription. It could not be otherwise. The will of Napoleon and Alexander (on whom the event seemed to depend) could be carried out only if innumerable circumstances came together, and if any one of them had been missing the event could not have taken place. The real power lay in the hands of millions of men — the soldiers who fired, or hauled provisions and guns — and they had to consent to carry out the will of these weak individuals. An infinite number of varied and complex causes had to bring them to it.

To explain irrational events (that is, events whose reasonableness we do not understand), we are forced to fall back on fatalism. The more we try to explain such events in history reasonably, the more unreasonable and incomprehensible they become to us.

Each man lives for himself, using his freedom to reach his personal aims, and feels with his whole being that he can do or not do this or that action right now. But as soon as he has done it, that action, performed at a certain moment in time, becomes irrevocable and belongs to history, where it has a significance that is not free but predestined.
Every man's life has two sides: his individual life, which is the more free the more abstract its interests, and his elemental hive life, in which he inevitably obeys laws laid down for him.

Man lives consciously for himself, but he is an unconscious instrument for achieving the historic, universal aims of humanity. A deed once done is irrevocable, and its result, coinciding in time with the actions of millions of other men, takes on historic significance. The higher a man stands on the social ladder, the more people he is connected with and the more power he has over others, the more evident is the predestination and inevitability of his every action.
"The king's heart is in the hands of the Lord."
A king is history's slave.
History — that is, the unconscious, general, hive life of mankind — uses every moment of a king's life as a tool for its own purposes.

Although Napoleon in 1812 was more convinced than ever that it depended on him, verser (ou ne pas verser) le sang de ses peuples * — as Alexander put it in the last letter he wrote him — he had never been so much in the grip of inevitable laws, which forced him, while he thought he was acting on his own volition, to do for the hive life — that is to say, for history — whatever had to be done.
* "To shed (or not to shed) the blood of his peoples."

The people of the west moved eastward to slay their fellow men, and by the law of coincidence thousands of tiny causes fitted together and combined to produce that movement and that war. There were reproaches for failing to observe the Continental System; the wrongs of the Duke of Oldenburg; the march of troops into Prussia, undertaken (as it seemed to Napoleon) only to secure an armed peace; the French Emperor's love and habit of war, which matched his people's inclinations; the lure of the grand preparations, the money spent on them, and the need to win advantages to make up for it; the intoxicating honors paid to him in Dresden; and the diplomatic negotiations, which in the opinion of contemporaries were carried on with a sincere desire for peace but only wounded the self-love of both sides. And there were millions of other causes that adapted themselves to the event that was happening or coincided with it.

When an apple has ripened and falls, why does it fall? Because it is pulled toward the earth, because its stalk withers, because the sun dries it, because it grows heavier, because the wind shakes it, or because the boy standing below wants to eat it?

Nothing is the cause. All this is only the coincidence of conditions under which every vital, organic, elemental event occurs. The botanist who finds that the apple falls because its cellular tissue decays, and so forth, is right, and so is the child standing under the tree who says it fell because he wanted to eat it and prayed for it. Equally right, or equally wrong, is the man who says that Napoleon went to Moscow because he wanted to and perished because Alexander desired his destruction, and the man who says that an undermined hill weighing a million tons fell because the last laborer struck it a final time with his pickax. In historic events the so-called great men are labels that give names to events, and like labels they have very little connection with the event itself.
Every act of theirs, which seems to them an act of their own will, is in an historical sense involuntary, is bound up with the whole course of history, and is predestined from eternity.
